opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is an interesting comparison, though you have to be careful not to over-read it. The rough picture is that DeepSeek-V3 was trained with something like a few times 10^24 FLOP, pretty modest by frontier standards, while Grok 3 was trained with maybe ten times that, or more depending on whose estimates you believe. And when you look at the base models, or at the non-reasoning versions, Grok 3 is better, but not dramatically better in the way you might naively expect from an order of magnitude more compute.

There are a few ways to interpret that. One is that the returns to pure pretraining scale are diminishing more than people expected, so you buy relatively less per order of magnitude now. I think there's probably something to that, though it's hard to separate from the other explanations.

The second, which I put a lot of weight on, is algorithmic efficiency. DeepSeek is a very strong team that squeezed a lot out of their compute with mixture-of-experts, multi-head latent attention, good data work, careful engineering. xAI was moving extremely fast and building a huge cluster quickly, and it's plausible they just weren't as compute-efficient. So part of the gap you'd expect from compute gets eaten by DeepSeek being maybe several times more efficient per FLOP. If that's right, the comparison tells you more about variance in algorithmic quality across labs than about the scaling curve itself.

Third, there's a measurement issue. The benchmarks we use are increasingly saturated or don't capture the things more pretraining compute buys you, like broader knowledge, better calibration, fewer weird failures, a vague sense of the model being smarter. Those are real but hard to see on standard evals.

So my overall take is that it's weak evidence that returns to pretraining compute alone are somewhat lower than a simple extrapolation would suggest, but mostly it's evidence that algorithmic progress and execution quality matter a lot, and that a strong team can be roughly an order of magnitude behind on compute and still be competitive. I don't think it means scaling is over. It's more consistent with a world where a lot of the action is shifting toward RL and post-training on top of decent base models, and where effective compute, meaning raw compute times algorithmic efficiency, is the thing to track rather than raw FLOP.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's actually a pretty interesting data point, though you have to be careful about how much you read into it.

So DeepSeek-V3 was trained with, by their own reporting, something like 2.8 million H800 hours, which works out to maybe $5 or $6 million of compute at market rates. And Grok 3, based on what xAI has said about their cluster, was trained with something like 100,000 H100s for a decent chunk of time. So we're talking about something like a 20x, maybe 30x, difference in pretraining compute, give or take, depending on how you account for things.

And then the question is: how much better is Grok 3? And my read is that Grok 3 is better. It's not like the gap is zero. But it's not dramatically better. If you look at benchmarks, if you look at Chatbot Arena, if you look at how people actually use these things, it's within the range where you could plausibly say, "OK, this is maybe one notch up, and a lot of the gap closes once DeepSeek does their reasoning model on top."

So one naive interpretation is: returns to pretraining compute are kind of bad. You put in 20x the compute and you get something that's a bit better. And I think that's partially right, but I'd want to make a couple of caveats.

The first is that DeepSeek is just unusually good at algorithmic efficiency. They did a bunch of things — the MLA attention, the fine-grained mixture of experts, the FP8 training, a lot of careful systems work — that mean they're getting more out of each FLOP than a typical lab would. So part of what you're seeing isn't "compute doesn't matter," it's "DeepSeek had a bunch of algorithmic advantages that are worth maybe a few x of compute." And xAI, being a newer org, plausibly was on the less efficient side. So the effective compute gap is smaller than the raw compute gap.

The second caveat is that the scaling laws we actually have predict that going up by 20x in compute gets you a noticeable but not transformational improvement. Like, if you think of each 10x as being roughly a "generation," then 20x is a bit more than one generation. And the GPT-3 to GPT-4 jump felt big to people, but that was more like 100x, plus a ton of post-training work. So I'd say the DeepSeek-V3 versus Grok 3 comparison is roughly consistent with what we'd expect from scaling laws — it's just that people have maybe miscalibrated expectations about how much a 20x should buy you.

The third thing is that Grok 3 was, as far as I can tell, somewhat rushed and maybe undertrained relative to what you could do with that compute. xAI brought up a huge cluster very quickly, and I would guess they didn't have as mature of a data pipeline and as mature a post-training stack as, say, OpenAI or Anthropic would have had with the same compute. So it's not a perfectly clean test of "what does 20x compute get you."

So, putting it together: I think it's moderate evidence that returns to raw pretraining compute are somewhat lower than the most bullish people thought, and moderate evidence that algorithmic progress is a really large fraction of what's driving capabilities right now. But I don't think it's evidence that scaling has "stopped working" or anything like that. It's more like: scaling works roughly as the scaling laws say, and that's just less dramatic per-order-of-magnitude than the vibes suggested, and labs that are good at algorithms can partially substitute for compute.

And then the interesting strategic implication is that if you think most of the gains are coming from algorithmic improvements and from RL on top of the base model, then the compute advantage of the leading labs is a bit less decisive than it would otherwise be, at least for now. Although I'd note that the RL side is itself getting pretty compute-hungry, so I expect compute to matter a lot going forward, just maybe in a somewhat different shape than pure pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s some evidence that the returns to scaling pretraining compute are relatively modest, but it’s a pretty noisy comparison. The basic observation is that Grok 3 appears to have used substantially more compute than DeepSeek-V3, without being overwhelmingly better. That should update you somewhat against the view that simply spending much more on pretraining reliably produces a dramatically more capable model.

But you’re comparing different organisations, with different data, architectures, and training recipes. DeepSeek could be doing a better job of using its compute. And you have to separate improvements from pretraining from improvements due to post-training or spending more compute at inference time, which is particularly important when comparing reasoning models.

So I wouldn’t conclude that scaling has stopped working. I’d conclude that this comparison is consistent with diminishing returns, and that algorithmic efficiency can compensate for a substantial compute gap. The cleaner evidence would be a series of runs using essentially the same recipe at different scales, rather than two headline models from different labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s some evidence that the returns to scaling pretraining compute are relatively modest, but it’s a pretty noisy comparison. The basic observation is that Grok 3 reportedly used substantially more compute than DeepSeek-V3, and it doesn’t seem correspondingly far ahead. If you thought that increasing pretraining compute by that much would reliably produce a dramatically more capable model, that should be an update against that view.

But it’s not a controlled experiment. The teams differ in their data, architecture, training methods, and post-training, and we don’t have a clean accounting of the compute that went into the particular models being compared. DeepSeek might simply have done a better job of using its compute. And benchmark performance isn’t a linear measure of capability, so a fairly small-looking difference in scores could still matter.

So I’d take it as a reason to be somewhat more skeptical of very large gains from pretraining scale alone, rather than as evidence that scaling has stopped working. It also leaves open how much progress you can get from better algorithms or from spending more compute during reasoning.
